title: Vectors and Vector Spaces
one_sentence_summary: Vectors and vector spaces provide the geometric language for representing data, features, and learned embeddings in machine learning.
quick_recall: A vector is an ordered list of numbers representing a point, direction, or feature pattern; a vector space is a set of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
big_picture: Machine learning usually works on numeric representations rather than raw objects. Vectors are the basic containers for those representations, and vector spaces specify the rules for combining and transforming them consistently. This lets us compare examples, learn embeddings, project data into lower dimensions, and reason about similarity and geometry in a way that supports many ML methods.
why_it_exists: We need vectors and vector spaces because ML must encode real-world objects into a form that computers can manipulate mathematically. Once information is represented as vectors, we can measure similarity, combine features, optimize models, and apply geometry-based methods like PCA or nearest-neighbor search.
intuition: Think of a vector as an arrow or coordinate point. In 2D, (2, 1) can mean 'move 2 units right and 1 unit up.' In ML, the same object can mean 'this example has two feature values.' A vector space is the whole room where such arrows live, and a subspace is a flat slice of that room. Linear combinations let us build new vectors from old ones, so a few basis vectors can describe many possibilities. That is why embeddings, hidden states, and feature spaces are so useful: they turn complicated data into geometry.
core_explanation:
A vector is an element of an ordered collection of numbers, often written as \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d)\) or as a column vector. The entries are coordinates in a chosen system, and the dimension \(d\) is the number of coordinates.

A vector space is a set of vectors together with two operations:
- vector addition: \(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}\)
- scalar multiplication: \(a\mathbf{x}\), where \(a\) is a number

The key idea is closure: if \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) are in the space, then \(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\) is also in the space, and if \(a\) is a scalar then \(a\mathbf{x}\) is also in the space. In ML, this matters because feature vectors, embeddings, and neural activations are designed so arithmetic on them is meaningful.

A linear combination is a sum of scaled vectors:
\(\alpha_1\mathbf{v}_1 + \alpha_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + \alpha_k\mathbf{v}_k\)
Here the \(\alpha_i\) are scalars, and the \(\mathbf{v}_i\) are vectors. Linear combinations describe what can be built from a set of vectors. The span of vectors is the set of all their linear combinations. If a set of vectors spans a space, then any vector in that space can be written using them.

A basis is a minimal set of vectors that spans the space and is linearly independent, meaning no basis vector is redundant. For \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the standard basis is \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\). Any 2D vector can be formed from them. The dimension is the number of vectors in a basis, so \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has dimension 2 and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) has dimension 3. In ML, high-dimensional spaces are common because each feature or embedding coordinate gives the model another axis along which examples can differ.

A subspace is a subset of a vector space that is itself a vector space. Geometrically, subspaces often look like lines or planes passing through the origin. In ML, subspaces show up when data live on a lower-dimensional structure inside a larger feature space, which is one reason dimensionality reduction can work.

The norm of a vector measures its size, often \(\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 = \sqrt{x_1^2 + \cdots + x_d^2}\). The dot product \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y} = \sum_i x_i y_i\) measures alignment. From it, cosine similarity is \(\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|\,\|\mathbf{y}\|}\), which compares direction while reducing sensitivity to overall scale. This is widely useful for embeddings, retrieval, and clustering.
mechanism:
In practice, an ML system converts each example into a vector:
- a tabular record becomes a feature vector
- a word or token becomes an embedding
- an image becomes a flattened or encoded representation
- a neural network layer produces an activation vector

Then the model processes these vectors with linear algebra: weighted sums, matrix multiplications, projections, and similarity calculations. Because vectors live in a vector space, these operations are predictable and composable.

A simple example is a linear model \(\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\). Here \(\mathbf{x}\) is the feature vector, \(\mathbf{w}\) is a learned direction, and the dot product measures how much the input aligns with that direction. In embedding models, semantically similar items are encouraged to have vectors that point in similar directions or lie near each other. In PCA, vectors are projected onto a lower-dimensional subspace that preserves as much variation as possible. In neural networks, each hidden layer transforms vectors into new vectors in another space, often making structure easier to separate or compare.

The geometric language helps explain model behavior: if two vectors are close under the similarity or distance measure used by the model, they may be treated as similar; if they lie in different directions, the model may separate them; if the data mostly vary along a few directions, a lower-dimensional basis may capture much of the signal.
ml_relevance: Vectors and vector spaces are central to ML because almost every model expects numeric arrays and learns by manipulating them. Feature engineering is vector design. Embeddings are learned vector representations. PCA is projection onto principal subspaces. Similarity search, clustering, and recommendation often depend on distances or angles between vectors. Even deep networks can be understood as repeated transformations between vector spaces.
practical_example:
Suppose we describe a movie with three features: \(\mathbf{x} = (\text{action}, \text{romance}, \text{comedy}) = (4, 1, 2)\). Another movie is \(\mathbf{y} = (3, 2, 2)\).

- The vectors represent feature strengths.
- The dot product tells us whether the movies are similar in a weighted sense.
- If we normalize them, cosine similarity focuses more on pattern than raw scale.
- A learned embedding might place similar movies near each other even if the original features are sparse or noisy.

For text, a word embedding like "king" or "queen" is also just a vector. The model does not need the vector to "look like" a word; it needs the geometry to encode useful relationships.

mathematical_foundation.overview: The mathematical core is the geometry of Euclidean vector spaces and the algebra of linear combinations. These ideas let us represent data, compare examples, and move between full spaces and lower-dimensional subspaces.

sections.title: Vectors as coordinates and arrows
sections.explanation: A vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is a list of \(d\) real numbers. The notation emphasizes that the vector is an object in a space, not just a table row. In 2D, \((x_1, x_2)\) can be drawn as an arrow from the origin to that point. In ML, the same object may represent a data sample, a feature vector, or an embedding.

equations.explanation: \(\mathbf{x}\) is a vector, \(x_1, \dots, x_d\) are its coordinates, and \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is the set of all real-valued vectors with \(d\) coordinates. This is the standard setting for ML feature vectors and embeddings.

This is the Euclidean norm, which measures vector length. It uses ordinary squared distance in each coordinate and is common in ML when comparing magnitude or using distance-based methods. The formula assumes real coordinates and the standard Euclidean geometry.

sections.title: Addition, scalar multiplication, and linear combinations
sections.explanation: Vector addition combines coordinates component-wise, and scalar multiplication rescales every coordinate. Together they allow linear combinations, which are the basic building blocks of spans, bases, and projections. In ML, weighted sums and matrix multiplications are built from these same operations.

equations.explanation: Adding vectors adds each coordinate separately. This is the simplest way to combine feature information or accumulate learned signals in a network layer.
Multiplying by a scalar stretches or shrinks a vector and can reverse its direction if \(a\) is negative. This is how ML weights can amplify, suppress, or flip features.

This linear combination builds a new vector from existing ones. The scalars \(\alpha_i\) control how much each direction contributes. Linear combinations are the algebraic language behind feature mixing, basis expansion, and linear layers.

sections.title: Span, basis, and dimension
sections.explanation: The span of vectors is everything you can reach by linear combinations. A basis is a smallest nonredundant spanning set. The dimension is the number of basis vectors, which tells you how many independent directions the space has. In ML, dimension is a practical measure of representational capacity.

equations.explanation: The span collects all vectors built from the chosen vectors using any real coefficients. If a dataset lies approximately in a low-dimensional span, compression or dimensionality reduction may be effective.

Here \(\mathbf{e}_i\) are basis vectors and \(c_i\) are coordinates of \(\mathbf{x}\) in that basis. This says every vector can be reconstructed from basis directions. In ML, learned bases or latent directions can provide compact descriptions.

The dimension of the standard real vector space \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is the number of independent coordinates. Higher dimension means more independent directions for variation, which can be powerful but also makes geometry less intuitive.

sections.title: Subspaces and projections
sections.explanation: A subspace is a vector space inside a larger vector space. Common examples are lines or planes through the origin. Projections map vectors onto a subspace and are central to PCA and many approximation methods.

equations.latex: S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ is a subspace if it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication}
equations.explanation: This describes the defining property of a subspace. Closure means that if you stay inside the subset and apply the vector-space operations, you do not leave it. In ML, this matters when data or model outputs are constrained to a structured family of directions.

This denotes the orthogonal projection of vector \(\mathbf{x}\) onto subspace \(S\). An orthogonal projection maps \(\mathbf{x}\) to the closest point in the subspace under Euclidean distance. PCA uses this idea to compress data while keeping important variation.

sections.title: Dot product and cosine similarity
sections.explanation: The dot product measures how much two vectors point in the same direction. Cosine similarity normalizes by vector length so it focuses on angle rather than scale. These are foundational for nearest-neighbor search, retrieval, clustering, and embedding comparison.

equations.explanation: The dot product multiplies corresponding coordinates and adds them up. It becomes large when vectors align and can be negative when they point in opposite directions. In ML, it underlies linear models and similarity scoring.

This converts the dot product into an angle-based similarity. The denominator removes the effect of vector length, so vectors with the same direction get similarity close to 1. This is useful when the direction of an embedding matters more than its magnitude.

common_misconceptions: A vector is not only an arrow on a graph; in ML it is usually a numeric representation in any dimension.
Higher-dimensional spaces are not just bigger 2D or 3D spaces; geometry changes in ways that affect distance, similarity, and intuition.
A basis is not the same as a general set of vectors; it must both span the space and be linearly independent.
Cosine similarity is not the same as Euclidean distance; one focuses on angle, the other on absolute position and scale.
A subspace does not have to be visually obvious; in high dimensions it can be hard to picture even when the math is simple.
limitations: Vector spaces describe representations, but they do not by themselves tell you which representation is semantically best.
Distance and angle are useful, but not every ML task is well captured by Euclidean geometry.
High dimensionality can make models expressive, but it can also make data sparse and comparisons less intuitive.
Real-world features may need normalization or careful preprocessing before vector geometry becomes meaningful.

deep_dive:
Vectors and vector spaces are the backbone of ML because they let us treat information geometrically. Once an object is encoded as a vector, it can be compared, transformed, compressed, and optimized with linear algebra. This geometric view is powerful because it is simple enough to compute with and expressive enough to represent complex patterns.

A useful way to think about ML is: choose a vector space, place examples in it, and then learn structure in that space. A classifier learns a separating direction or surface. A recommender learns user and item embeddings so that compatible vectors are nearby. A language model maps tokens into hidden vectors and repeatedly transforms them so that useful information becomes easier to extract.

The more dimensions a space has, the more independent features it can express. But high dimension also means that intuition from 2D can fail. Distances may behave differently, many directions may be nearly orthogonal, and data may occupy only a small structured region. That is why basis, dimension, subspace, and projection are not just abstract linear algebra ideas; they are tools for understanding model capacity, compression, and representation learning.

In short: vector spaces are the mathematical stage on which much of machine learning happens.
